problem: Existing robot navigation systems cannot use human-oriented wayfinding resources such as room labels, directional signs and asking people for directions, so they explore large man-made buildings inefficiently.
motivation: Buildings are designed for humans to navigate with signs and room-numbering patterns, and a wrong exploration direction in an 80m+ building costs a lot of time. VLMs can read text and reason, but they handle spatial data and numeric outputs poorly, so compact input and output abstractions are needed.
key_idea: Represent the scene as a memory bank of landmarks (frontiers, doors, people, signs) with attached text, and let a zero-shot VLM pick the next landmark to visit, which triggers predefined behavior primitives such as sign reading, room-label reading and asking for directions.
insight: Both the skills and the input abstraction matter. Removing sign and people feedback drops real-world success to 8.3% (vs 58.3%) and simulation to 42.86% (vs 57.14%). Removing the map image drops simulation success to 14.29%, and removing the JSON landmark memory drops it to 0 because the VLM keeps re-choosing visited landmarks. The VLM also beats non-VLM heuristics (closest 35.71%, random 28.57%), so the reasoning over signs, numbering patterns and human hints adds real value.
method: Low-level stream: 2D SLAM (SLAM Toolbox) from 3D lidar, NanoOWL open-vocabulary detection of door/person/directions sign, VLFM-style frontier extraction, Nav2 NavFn planner with an MPPI controller.

Landmark memory bank: JSON of indexed doors, people, signs and frontiers, each marked Visited/Unvisited, with attached room-label text, sign directions in cardinal bins, or VLM-written notes from people.
Top-down map visualization: a north-up occupancy/explored map with landmark symbols and index numbers, given to the VLM (GPT-4.1) together with the JSON.
VLM landmark selection: the VLM reasons step by step (sign directions, ascending/descending door-number patterns, asking nearby people) and outputs a landmark index rather than coordinates.

Behavior primitives: frontier = go and turn 360°; door = approach, pan the camera, detect and read the room label with the VLM; sign = read it and convert arrows to global cardinal directions; person = text-to-speech question, speech-to-text answer, and a VLM note in cardinal directions.
Isaac Sim hospital benchmark: 30+ rooms, signs, 11 NPCs with hard-coded knowledge bases, and a ROS2 interface shared with the real robot.

setting.backbone: GPT-4.1 (frozen, via API) plus NanoOWL/OWL-ViT detector (no retraining)
setting.observation: RGB-D pan-tilt camera (used for detection and text reading only), 3D+2D lidar for SLAM, microphone speech
setting.action_space: high-level landmark selection executed by Nav2 point-goal planning (NavFn + MPPI) and behavior primitives
setting.simulator: Isaac Sim (custom hospital) plus real world
setting.privileged: none (in sim, NPCs give hard-coded conversational responses)

numbers.eval_set_note: 12 real-world trials (10 in building A, 2 in building B)
numbers.extra: 15-minute limit; failures assigned 900s and 100m; per-building durations and distances are in the table
numbers.evidence: Table 1: Quantitative Results for Navigation in Real-World Environments; Ours avg 58.3
Table 2: Quantitative Results for Navigation in Simulation Environments (Large Hospital)

numbers_note: Only the authors' own custom real-world and Isaac Sim benchmarks; no standard benchmark. Trial counts are small (12 real, 14 sim).
results: Full system reaches 58.3% real-world success (12 trials) and 57.14% in simulation (14 trials), outperforming the No Signs/People ablation (8.3% real, 42.86% sim) and the No Map Image ablation (16.6% real, 14.29% sim). It also beats no-VLM heuristics in simulation (closest 35.71%, random 28.57%), with lower time and distance.
limitations: Performance is bottlenecked by the object detector: incorrect or missed detections make up most real-world failures, e.g. posters detected as signs.
The VLM sees only landmarks and is restricted to frontier targets, so it does not fully use camera information or choose closer waypoints.
Small evaluation (12 real and 14 sim trials) on custom environments, with no dynamic-actor handling, no reasoning about which human is more informative, and Nav2 planner failures in narrow halls.
